hints: Look at the Period 3 elements and ask yourself which one reacts rapidly with water to give an alkaline hydroxide.
That behaviour points to sodium, so the chloride you are asked about is $\text{NaCl}$, a typical Group 1 metal chloride.
Now compare ionic chlorides with covalent chlorides for melting point, molten conductivity and reaction with water to pick the true property.
walkthrough:
**Identify element X**

Think like a detective. Period 3 goes $\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$, $\text{Al}$, $\text{Si}$, $\text{P}$, $\text{S}$, $\text{Cl}$, $\text{Ar}$. Only sodium reacts rapidly and violently with cold water to form an alkaline solution.

$$2\text{Na} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2$$

**Work out the bonding in its chloride**

So X is sodium and its chloride is $\text{NaCl}$. A Group 1 metal plus a non-metal means electron transfer, so it is a giant ionic lattice, not a simple covalent molecule.

$$\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+ + e^-, \quad \text{Cl} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}^-$$

**Apply ionic properties**

Ionic lattices have very high melting points (about $801^\circ\text{C}$ for $\text{NaCl}$), conduct electricity when molten or aqueous because ions are free to move, but do not conduct as solids. They simply dissolve in water, they do not hydrolyse rapidly like $\text{SiCl}_4$ or $\text{PCl}_3$ do. That matches only one statement.

options.A: Correct. Molten $\text{NaCl}$ contains mobile $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, so it conducts electricity. This is characteristic of a giant ionic chloride.
options.B: False. Ionic $\text{NaCl}$ has strong electrostatic attractions in a giant lattice, so its melting point is very high, about $801^\circ\text{C}$. A melting point below $100^\circ\text{C}$ would suggest a simple covalent chloride such as $\text{PCl}_3$.
options.C: False. $\text{NaCl}$ has ionic bonding by electron transfer from Na to Cl. Covalent bonding is found in the non-metal chlorides on the right of Period 3, such as $\text{SiCl}_4$.
options.D: False. $\text{NaCl}$ just dissolves in water to give neutral hydrated ions, it does not hydrolyse. Rapid reaction with cold water to give acidic fumes is typical of covalent chlorides like $\text{SiCl}_4$ and $\text{PCl}_5$.
